1b7cfe245ce32f: The Constitution: your most important rights document
01c5218ca677ae: Article 1 and the 2011 human rights reform — the foundation for everything else in this course.
079a25f7e76f60:
The country's highest law

The Political Constitution of the United Mexican States is the country's supreme law — no other law, regulation or authority can validly contradict it. Its first articles hold the most fundamental rights of every person on Mexican territory.

Article 1: the entry point

Article 1 establishes that all people enjoy the human rights recognized both in the Constitution and in international treaties signed by Mexico, and that all discrimination is prohibited based on ethnic origin, gender, age, disability, social status, religion, opinions, sexual preferences, marital status, or anything else that undermines human dignity.

📜 An important fact: in 2011 there was a constitutional reform that significantly expanded Article 1, requiring every authority in the country to interpret human rights in the way that most protects the person (the "pro persona" principle), rather than just applying the law literally when that would reduce protection.

Mexican person, or any person?

A point that surprises many: most constitutional rights apply to every person on Mexican territory, not just those with Mexican nationality. There are specific exceptions (like the right to vote), but rights like due process or the prohibition of discrimination protect anyone, regardless of nationality.

💡 Throughout this course you'll see references to specific articles (3, 4, 20, 123) — each one covers a different area of your life: education, health, criminal process, and work, respectively.

16fffa0e378cb1: Work hours, rest, the year-end bonus, vacation and social security — what the law guarantees you as a worker.
07633fc9aaaa9a:
The article that protects your job

Article 123 of the Constitution, along with the Federal Labor Law (LFT) that develops it, establishes the minimum rights of any working person in Mexico, regardless of the type of job.

Rights you probably already have, even if you don't know it

  • Maximum shift length: 8 hours for the day shift, 7 for the night shift, 7.5 for a mixed shift — weekly totals shouldn't exceed certain limits, and overtime pays more than regular hours.
  • Weekly rest: at least one full day off for every six days worked.
  • Year-end bonus (aguinaldo): a mandatory annual payment equal to a minimum of 15 days' pay, which must be paid before December 20 each year — regardless of the type of contract.
  • Paid vacation: every worker is entitled to a paid vacation period that increases with seniority, starting from the first year worked.
  • Social security (IMSS): your employer is required to enroll you in the Mexican Social Security Institute, giving you access to medical care, paid disability leave, and a future pension.
  • Profit sharing (PTU): companies with profits must distribute a percentage among their workers every year.
⚠️ The exact amounts (like the minimum wage) change every year — this course doesn't give you specific figures so it doesn't go out of date. What doesn't change is that these rights EXIST and can't be validly waived, not even if your employer asks you to "sign" that you're giving them up.

A right that surprises many people

📝 These rights apply even without a written contract. A real employment relationship (where someone gives you instructions, a schedule and pay in exchange for your work) generates these rights automatically by law, whether or not there's a signed document — though having the written contract always makes them easier to defend.
💡 If you think your employer is violating any of these rights, the path is the Conciliation and Arbitration Board (or the new Labor Conciliation Centers, under the ongoing labor reform) — you'll see more about where to go in module 6.

11d1ea08f026a6: Your rights if authorities detain you
0fe2e782e8bafe: Article 20 of the Constitution and the basic protections against police and the criminal justice system — information that can make a real difference.
07510af0e44ef0:
The most urgent article to know

Article 20 of the Constitution establishes the rights of any person within a criminal proceeding — from the moment of an arrest through trial. Knowing it doesn't make you guilty of anything; it protects you even if you're completely innocent.

Your basic rights during an arrest

  • Presumption of innocence: you're considered innocent until a judge determines otherwise at trial — the authority has to prove your guilt, not you your innocence.
  • Right to remain silent: you're not required to say anything, and your silence can't be used against you.
  • Right to a lawyer: from the moment of arrest, including a free public defender if you can't afford one.
  • Right to be informed clearly of the reasons for your arrest and the charges against you.
  • Right to communicate: to let someone you trust know about your arrest and where you are.
  • Legal time limits: there are constitutional time limits for authorities to bring you before a judge or prosecutor — they can't hold you indefinitely without due process.
  • Right to an interpreter or translator if you don't speak Spanish or belong to an Indigenous community and need to communicate in your own language.
⚠️ These rights exist in the law — that doesn't always guarantee they're perfectly respected in practice in every case. That's exactly why it's important to know them: so you can identify and report it when they aren't upheld (see module 5, on the CNDH).
🎓 A practical and legal tip: staying calm, being respectful, and clearly saying "I want to exercise my right to remain silent and to have a lawyer present" is a legal and effective way to protect your rights without confrontation, whether you're guilty or innocent.
💡 These rights apply to anyone in Mexico, regardless of nationality — as you saw in module 1.

11eed294dba472: Health, education and housing: social rights
13f32aa0d39988: Articles 3 and 4 of the Constitution — rights the State has an obligation to progressively guarantee.
04d4b02136fae0:
Rights that require the State to act

Unlike rights that protect you from the State doing something wrong (like arresting you without cause), social rights require the State to actively do something to guarantee you a dignified life.

Article 3: education

It establishes that every person has the right to receive an education, and that education provided by the State will be free, secular and mandatory from preschool through upper-secondary education (high school). "Secular" means public education can't be oriented toward any particular religion.

Article 4: one article, many rights

This article, expanded through several reforms over the years, brings together several important social rights:

  • Equality between women and men before the law.
  • The right to decide freely, responsibly and with full information on the number and spacing of one's children.
  • The right to health protection — including access to health services, though actual quality and coverage vary depending on the system (IMSS, ISSSTE, state services).
  • The right to a healthy environment for development and well-being.
  • The right to water that is sufficient, safe and accessible.
  • The right to dignified and decent housing.
  • The right to identity and to be registered from birth.
⚠️ Social rights are usually described as subject to "progressive realization" — meaning the State has an obligation to move toward fully meeting them with the resources available, which doesn't always mean they're 100% guaranteed in practice for everyone. That gap between the right on paper and reality is, in fact, an area of constant public debate.
💡 Knowing these rights gives you concrete language to demand improvements — not as a favor from the government, but as something the Constitution already recognizes as yours.

0951d64f7fbcf9: The CNDH: what to do if an authority violates your rights
0185b1dfe27cf5: How the National Human Rights Commission works, and the key difference between a CNDH complaint and a criminal report.
094323e49d1e07:
An agency built exactly for this

The National Human Rights Commission (CNDH) is the autonomous body responsible for receiving and addressing complaints about alleged human rights violations committed by authorities or public officials — not by private individuals. Every state also has its own state human rights commission, which handles cases within its jurisdiction.

Key difference: human rights complaint vs. criminal report

⚖️ They're not the same thing: if a police officer physically assaults you without cause, you can (and maybe should) do both things separately: (1) file a complaint with the CNDH or your state commission over the violation of your human rights, which can lead to recommendations to the institution, and (2) file a criminal report with the prosecutor's office over the specific crime (assault, abuse of authority), seeking legal sanctions against the person responsible. They're different processes, with different goals, and you can use both.

What kinds of cases does the CNDH handle?

  • Arbitrary detentions or excessive use of force by authorities.
  • Medical negligence in public health institutions.
  • Discrimination by public officials.
  • Undignified conditions in detention centers.
  • Due process violations by authorities.

What the CNDH does NOT do

⚠️ The CNDH doesn't resolve conflicts between private individuals (two neighbors, a private employer and employee with no State involvement), and its recommendations aren't direct criminal penalties — they're public recommendations to the responsible authority, with moral and political weight, but not always guaranteed compliance. For labor or civil conflicts between private parties, the path is different (see module 2 and the Introduction to Law course).
💡 Filing a complaint with the CNDH or your state commission is usually free and doesn't require a lawyer — it's one of the most accessible ways to exercise your rights against an authority that overstepped.

0902944f7c0b85: Consumer rights: PROFECO and the basics you should know
1c28950444886f: What the law protects you against when you buy a product or hire a service, and where to go if you get ripped off.
1b072cb8a67ad3:
The agency that protects you as a consumer

The Federal Consumer Protection Agency (PROFECO) is the institution responsible for protecting consumers' rights against companies and providers of goods and services in Mexico.

Basic rights you probably already have

  • Right to truthful information: a product's advertising and labeling can't be misleading.
  • Right to an invoice or receipt for any purchase you make.
  • Right to a warranty on products, according to the period set by the manufacturer or the law.
  • Protection against abusive clauses in adhesion contracts (those long contracts you "accept" without negotiating, like phone or financial service contracts).
  • Right to cancel certain purchases within a specific window, in cases like door-to-door sales or remote purchases, according to applicable law.
🛒 A common case: if you buy a product and it doesn't work correctly within the warranty period, you have the right to demand a repair, replacement, or refund — the company can't simply refuse without legal justification.

How to file a complaint

PROFECO offers a free conciliation process: you file your complaint, the company is notified, and an agreement between both parties is sought with the agency's mediation — no lawyer or lawsuit needed.

⚠️ PROFECO protects consumer relationships (you as a buyer, a company as a seller) — it doesn't apply to conflicts between two private individuals that aren't formal businesses, nor to very specific financial services that have their own protection agency (CONDUSEF).
💡 Keeping your invoices and purchase receipts isn't just being organized — it's literally the evidence you need if you ever have to exercise these rights.

0b1715369b8063: The amparo: the most powerful tool almost no one knows about
0040fd32d9b29b: A unique Mexican legal mechanism that lets you defend yourself directly when a law or an act of authority violates your rights.
054a568ccdf1da:
A legal tool unique to Mexico

The amparo trial is one of the most important rights-protection mechanisms in the Mexican legal system — and, surprisingly, little known by most of the population, despite having existed for more than a century and a half.

What is it for?

An amparo lets you go before a federal judge to request protection when you believe a law, an act, or an omission by an authority violates your human rights or guarantees recognized in the Constitution or international treaties. If the judge rules in your favor, they order that law or act to stop applying to your specific case (or, in certain broader cases, more generally).

⚖️ Examples of when an amparo is used:
  • An authority denies you a procedure you're entitled to, without valid legal justification.
  • A newly passed law violates a specific constitutional right of yours.
  • An act by an authority (a fine, a closure, a suspension) was carried out without following due process.

Do you need a lawyer to file one?

Technically, anyone can file an amparo on their own in certain cases, but in practice it's a technical and complex process — the vast majority of successful amparos are filed with help from a specialized lawyer, or through a public defender's office in qualifying cases.

⚠️ An amparo isn't automatically free or instant — it has strict deadlines (often very short, a matter of days) for filing after the act you're challenging, so if you think you have a case, how quickly you seek advice matters a lot.
💡 Just knowing this tool exists already gives you an advantage: many people assume there's nothing to be done against an unjust act of authority, when in reality the Mexican legal system does provide a formal way to challenge it.

1b31686536f2a6:
What you covered

You started with the foundation for everything: Article 1 and why rights protect "every person" (class 1). You saw your labor rights (class 2), your protections during an arrest (class 3), the social rights to health, education and housing (class 4), where to go if an authority violates your rights (class 5), your rights as a consumer (class 6), and one of the most powerful and least-known legal tools in the Mexican system: the amparo (class 7).

The real goal of this course

It was never about memorizing article numbers — it was about knowing these rights exist, that they don't depend on someone doing you a favor, and that there are concrete paths (CNDH, PROFECO, public defender, amparo) to exercise them when you need them.

🧭 Your "where to go" checklist, in one place:
  • Did an authority violate your rights? → CNDH or your state human rights commission.
  • A crime committed against you? → Prosecutor's Office.
  • Labor conflict? → Conciliation and Arbitration Board / Labor Conciliation Centers.
  • Problem with a company as a consumer? → PROFECO.
  • Need to challenge a law or act of authority? → Amparo trial, with help from a lawyer or public defender.
⚠️ The final, most important reminder: this course is general civic education, not legal advice for your specific case. Laws change, amounts change, and every real situation has details only a professional can properly evaluate. But now you have something you might not have had before: the map for knowing where to start, instead of depending entirely on someone else explaining it to you once it's already urgent.
💡 If you enjoyed thinking about rights and justice more broadly, the "Introduction to Law" course (if you haven't taken it yet) and "My Rights as a Canadian" in this same school give you more context and comparison.
